channel.title: Counterwise — new guides and picks
channel.description: Kitchen gear, chosen by question rather than by hype.

item.title: The comparison table, with deliberate blanks
item.description: Five products compared on the fields stable enough to print. Two columns are empty and the reason is written underneath.

item.title: Five products, and what each one is for
item.description: Three air fryers and two thermometers that solve different problems, each with the same page structure.

item.title: Two baskets or one: does your weeknight actually have two foods in it?
item.description: A dual basket is not a bigger air fryer, it is two smaller ones that finish together. Look at the meal you actually cook before you decide which of those you want.

item.title: Dishwasher-safe does not mean dishwasher-sized: how do you check before you buy?
item.description: A coating rating and a rack are two different facts. What the listings say, what they do not say, and the four-part count that tells you what a night of cleanup will actually cost.

item.title: Do you need a connected probe for a holiday turkey, or just a thermometer?
item.description: The hard part of a holiday roast is not accuracy, it is attention. What a WiFi probe adds, what it does not, and the two-minute test to run before the day you cannot afford to be surprised.

item.title: Air fryer or toaster oven: can a tape measure settle it before you buy?
item.description: Before you compare watts or presets, three numbers on your own counter decide most of it. Here is the measuring method, and what the listings on this site deliberately do not state.

item.title: Air-fryer leftovers: what reheats safely?
item.description: Leftovers and casseroles have a USDA minimum of 165°F. An air fryer is a good reheater and a bad guesser — here is how to reheat to the number, not to “hot”.

item.title: Game-day wings: one big basket or two small ones?
item.description: One tray of wings for sharing, not two small ones — one basket or two? The answer is arithmetic on stated capacities, plus one question about sauce.

item.title: Holiday roast thermometer: instant-read or leave-in?
item.description: A whole bird, a rest, and a safe leftover — which thermometer job is this? The USDA minimums and the rest time decide which tool earns its drawer.

item.title: Wings for a crowd: the capacity arithmetic to do before game day
item.description: Party food is a surface-area problem wearing a volume costume. A short method — one bag of frozen wings, a tape measure and honest counting — that tells you how many batches a crowd really takes, and when a bigger machine would not have helped.

item.title: Smart meat thermometers: the questions to ask before you pay for a radio
item.description: A leave-in probe buys you a temperature graph and costs you an app. Before comparing models, decide which of those two facts matters more in your kitchen — the spec sheet will not decide it for you.

item.title: Hosting this winter: which air fryer format fits the meal you actually cook?
item.description: The oven is full, the guests are early, and the machine on the counter is either saving dinner or getting in the way. A format-first way to decide what kind of air fryer a hosting household actually needs — before the season decides for you.

item.title: Is your thermometer telling the truth? The two-minute ice test
item.description: A thermometer can be fast, waterproof and beautifully made and still read wrong. The USDA food-safety agency publishes a two-minute check that catches a drifting thermometer before it ruins a roast — this page walks through it, and through what a failure means.

item.title: Five gifts for the cook who already has an oven: match the person, not the preset count
item.description: A gift guide with no prices and no star ratings — those live on the listing and change too fast to reprint. What stays stable is fit: which of these five units suits which kind of cook, and the three checks to run before wrapping any of them.

item.title: Hosting season: which machine cooks what on the big day?
item.description: One oven, four side dishes and a guest list. The December problem is oven occupancy, not appliance quality: a job-by-job way to split the cooking across a countertop oven, a dual basket and a big single basket, with the safety numbers that decide when each job is done.

item.title: What temperature is actually “done”? A thermometer guide
item.description: The USDA publishes safe minimum internal temperatures. This page gathers them in one place, explains the rest time, and sets out what a thermometer has to do to be useful for them.

item.title: Questions to ask before buying a multi-function appliance
item.description: Twenty-four presets is not a feature list; it is a menu. The useful question is which three modes you will actually use, and what each one replaces.

item.title: Cleanup and counter space: the trade-offs to assess
item.description: The two costs nobody compares when they buy an air fryer: how much of the sink it takes, and how much of the counter it permanently occupies.

item.title: A no-hype checklist for comparing air fryer capacity
item.description: Manufacturers quote quarts. Food occupies space. This is a short method for closing the gap between the two before you buy, using a tape measure and one bag of frozen chips.

item.title: Basket or oven-style air fryer: what should you compare?
item.description: Two machines, both called air fryers, doing different jobs. The comparison that matters is not capacity in quarts — it is how you get food in and out, and where the machine lives when you are not using it.
